name: Quasi-count Plural Noun

1.definition: Denotes aggregates of discrete individuals with weakened individuation, yielding a mixed countability profile

constraints.description: Plural-only morphology with plural agreement; resists singular and a/an.
Individuation is weakened; tight count properties (low cardinals, distributives) are degraded.
Tight cardinality uses surface mainly in specialized registers.

relatedConstructions.notes: Many cattle has a lexically restricted plural count profile. Some rabbit uses a noun productively in non-count syntax to refer to material.

core.property: Plural-only morphology with loose count diagnostics

stabilisers.evidence: High-frequency quasi-count lexemes stabilize the profile.
Singulative reference is offloaded to functional alternatives (cow, officer).
Iterated transmission preserves the ordered dissociation pattern.

projection.target: Cattle admits many and plural agreement, while an individual count normally uses a classifier or counting expression such as three head of cattle. No claim about novel forms follows automatically from those facts.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the restricted cardinal patterns and plural agreement of plural-only nouns.

perturbations: Loss of functional singulatives pushes toward full count or non-count profiles.

coupling.mechanism: bidirectional inference between construal and count morphosyntax

curious.title: Plural words with no single form
curious.summary: Some nouns, such as cattle, are plural in form with no singular, and only partly behave like ordinary count nouns.
curious.body: Cattle works with many and takes plural verbs: many cattle. But it has no singular, and a cattle isn't something you say. These nouns refer to groups of separate individuals, yet they don't let us pick out one at a time in the usual way. To count individuals, English uses a counting expression such as three head of cattle, or a different word altogether, like cow. This dictionary marks the account as provisional, though it treats the pattern as stable.
curious.try: Try saying a cattle and then a cow. Which one lets you talk about a single animal? What would you say for several?

teacher.summary: Low priority for most classes: cattle is relatively infrequent (about 3,700th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts), so treat it if it comes up rather than teaching it. Explains plural-only nouns like cattle that take many but resist a, one and low numbers.
teacher.explain: Quasi-count plural nouns are plural-only, with plural agreement, and resist singular forms and a/an. They allow loose count diagnostics (many, few, high round numerals) but tight ones (a/an, low cardinals, distributives) are degraded. Individuals are counted with specialized frames such as three head of cattle, or by a different word (cow, officer). Tight cardinality uses surface mainly in specialized registers. This dictionary marks the account provisional and says no claim about novel forms follows automatically. Folks is a boundary item showing instability.
teacher.terms: Related to plural-only or collective nouns in traditional grammars; this dictionary calls these quasi-count nouns, with a mixed countability profile.
watch_for: A learner might think three cattle is the standard way to count three animals, when this dictionary gives three head of cattle.
A learner might use a with cattle to refer to a single animal.
A learner might treat all plural-only nouns as having the same profile.
teacher.activity: If cattle comes up in a reading, students list plural-only nouns they know and test each with many, a and three, recording which tests fit.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary now opens by marking the entry low priority (cattle about 3,700th in SUBTLEX-UK); activity, which tests plural-only nouns students know, now starts from cattle coming up in a reading.
